item.title: Sidecars and exam days: two Korean market quirks explained as the KOSPI slides 4%
item.description:
A sidecar on a 4% down day signals forced or automated selling at pace, and traders will watch whether the pause steadies futures or merely delays further losses. Korea’s heavy weighting in chipmakers leaves it exposed to any extension of the overnight rotation out of AI-linked stocks, with knock-on effects for regional tech and the won. A weaker won could add to the pressure if foreign investors keep selling.

The November 19 timetable is a minor liquidity consideration, but one that can catch out overseas desks used to the normal opening time.

---

Korea hit the brakes on its trading algorithms today, and in two weeks it will hit pause for its students.

Summary:

  • The KOSPI fell around 4% on Thursday, and a sidecar briefly suspended program trading tied to KOSPI 200 futures
  • A sidecar halts program orders for five minutes when futures move sharply and stay there for a minute; normal trading continues
  • The slide coincided with an overnight selloff in AI and chip stocks on Wall Street
  • On November 19, KOSPI and KOSDAQ trading will open at 10:00 local time (01:00 GMT) and close at 16:30 (07:30 GMT), an hour later than usual
  • The delay is for the Suneung university entrance exam, when offices start late, flights pause and police help students reach exam halls

South Korea’s stock market offered a crash course in two of its more unusual mechanisms on Thursday. As the KOSPI slid around 4%, a “sidecar” briefly paused automated trading, while the exchange announced it will open an hour late later this month so students can get to their university entrance exams on time.

The sidecar came first. It is a circuit breaker for program trading: when KOSPI 200 futures move sharply against the previous close and stay there for a minute, the exchange suspends computer-driven program orders for five minutes. On the main board the trigger is a 5% move. Ordinary trading continues, but the pause is designed to stop automated selling or buying from feeding on itself during a fast market. A sidecar can only be triggered once a day.

Thursday’s slide coincided with a sharp selloff in AI and chip stocks on Wall Street overnight, a theme that weighs heavily on Korea given the index’s exposure to semiconductor makers.

The second quirk is gentler. The Korea Exchange said trading on the KOSPI and KOSDAQ will start at 10:00 local time on November 19 (01:00 GMT, or 20:00 ET on November 18), an hour later than usual, and close at 16:30 (07:30 GMT, 02:30 ET). After-hours trading will also shift an hour later, running from 17:00 to 20:00.

The reason is the Suneung, the national university entrance exam, which is treated as close to a national event. Results play a major role in which universities students can enter, and with around half a million candidates sitting it each year, the country rearranges itself around the day. Government offices and many companies delay their start times to keep roads clear, aircraft take-offs and landings are typically halted during the English listening section, and police stand by to rush late students to exam halls.

For investors trading Korea from overseas, both are worth knowing. A sidecar is a signal that futures are moving fast, while the exam-day timetable shifts when Korean price action feeds into the rest of the Asian session. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of England preview: first hike to 4% expected as energy pushes inflation to 3.5%
item.description:
With a hike almost fully priced, sterling’s reaction will hinge on the vote split and guidance, with a 7-2 outcome and cautious language the most likely route to a softer pound. Gilts could rally if the Bank pushes back on market pricing for several more hikes, particularly at the short end. Oil is the swing factor beyond today: renewed strength in crude and gas would keep pressure on the Bank to tighten further, while any easing in Middle East tensions would weaken the case for a second move. The updated inflation projections will be scrutinised for how much of the energy shock the Bank expects to persist into 2027.

-

The Bank of England is set to hike; what it says about the next one will matter more.

Summary:

  • The BoE is widely expected to lift Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%, at 12:00 GMT (07:00 ET)
  • It held at 3.75% in September in a 6-3 vote, with three members favouring a hike
  • UK CPI rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1%, driven by fuel costs
  • Goldman Sachs expects a 7-2 vote, with the committee ready to respond but giving no strong steer
  • Many economists see one more hike, to 4.25%, early next year, less than markets price
  • New forecasts are likely to show inflation peaking above 4% in early 2027

The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates on Thursday for the first time in this cycle, lifting Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4% as energy costs push UK inflation further above target, with the decision due at 12:00 GMT (07:00 ET).

The move would follow a closely divided September meeting, when the Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% in a 6-3 vote, with three members already favouring a rise to 4%. Since then, the inflation picture has deteriorated. Consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and higher than expected, driven largely by rising fuel costs.

Markets have almost fully priced in a hike, and research houses are close to unanimous. Goldman Sachs expects a 7-2 vote in favour, a split shared by much of the consensus, with the two likely dissenters preferring to hold. Some forecasters see a narrower margin.

The more important question for markets is what comes next. Money markets have priced in several further increases over the coming year, a path many economists consider too aggressive. The more common base case is one additional quarter-point rise early next year, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%, possibly in February, when inflation is projected to peak. Goldman expects the committee to signal readiness to respond if inflation pressure builds, but without a strong steer on future meetings.

This is also a forecast meeting, with the Bank publishing an updated Monetary Policy Report. Its new projections are likely to show a higher near-term inflation peak in the first half of 2027, with Goldman expecting it at above 4%. Oil and gas prices are now running above the adverse scenario the Bank set out in July, raising the risk that the Middle East conflict leaves a more lasting mark on UK inflation.

That is the central concern for the hawks. Underlying measures remain firm, with services inflation approaching 4%, and the key risk is that higher energy costs become embedded in wages and price-setting. Against that, wage growth has been described as soft and the consumer is under pressure, giving the doves grounds for caution.

For sterling and gilts, the guidance and vote split are likely to matter more than the hike itself. A cautious message alongside a widely expected increase could see markets pare back their more aggressive pricing, while any sign of a faster pace would reinforce it. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Berkshire adds $27 million of Sirius XM as investors rotate from AI toward value stocks
item.description:
A Berkshire purchase tends to act as a sentiment signal for the target stock, which may help sustain Sirius XM’s rally as long as the broader rotation holds. More widely, it adds a high-profile example to the case for cash-generative, buyback-heavy companies at a time when investors are questioning returns on AI spending. Other mature media and consumer names with strong free cash flow could draw interest on the same logic. If AI stocks rebound quickly, though, the appetite for value plays may fade as fast as it arrived.

--- While the market argues over AI spending, Berkshire is quietly buying a company that hands cash back to shareholders.

Summary:

  • Berkshire bought about 924,000 Sirius XM shares for roughly $27 million from October 30 to November 3, per a regulatory filing
  • Its stake is now about 125.7 million shares, roughly 37% of the company, held mainly through GEICO
  • It paid about $29 to $30 a share, versus about $21 to $22 in mid-2025
  • The buying followed Q3 results in which Sirius XM raised full-year guidance and flagged faster buybacks in 2027
  • It coincides with a broad rotation out of AI infrastructure stocks, though the purchases predate Wednesday’s selloff

Berkshire Hathaway has added to its stake in Sirius XM, buying about $27 million of shares over three trading days, a modest purchase for the conglomerate but one that lines up with a broader shift in investor appetite toward cash-generating, value-oriented stocks.

According to a regulatory filing, Berkshire bought about 924,000 Sirius XM shares between October 30 and November 3, lifting its holding to about 125.7 million shares. Most of the stake is held through insurer GEICO, with the rest in Berkshire subsidiary pension plans. Based on Sirius XM’s market value of about $11.2 billion, that equates to roughly 37% of the company.

The buying came at higher prices than Berkshire’s previous reported purchases. It paid an average of roughly $29 to $30 a share, compared with about $21 to $22 when it last added to the position in mid-2025, and it kept buying as the stock rose. Sirius XM shares have gained about 13% over the past week, closing at around $33 on Wednesday.

The purchases followed Sirius XM’s third-quarter results on October 29. Revenue was broadly flat and earnings came in slightly below forecasts, but the company raised its full-year guidance for a second consecutive quarter, reported a 14% rise in free cash flow and said it expects to step up share buybacks significantly in 2027. The risks have not gone away: listener numbers at its Pandora service fell, leverage is elevated and management expects a tougher fourth quarter for subscribers.

The wider market context gives the move added resonance. On Wednesday, US stocks rallied broadly while investors rotated out of AI infrastructure names, with the Dow surging about 1,570 points even as Nvidia and other chip stocks fell. Research houses including UBS have been urging investors to trim concentrated technology exposure, while others have warned that the AI spending cycle may be peaking.

Berkshire’s purchases predate that selloff, so they are not a reaction to it. But a bet on a mature, cash-rich business returning capital to shareholders sits squarely on the other side of the AI capex trade that has dominated markets this year.

Whether the rotation lasts will shape how much attention such value plays attract. For now, Berkshire’s willingness to pay up signals continued conviction in Sirius XM, even after a sharp rally. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia’s trade surplus jumps to A$2.8 billion, a seven-month high, on LNG and metals
item.description:
A stronger trade surplus is modestly supportive for the Australian dollar, reinforcing the currency’s link to commodity prices. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth.

--

Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest.

Summary:

  • Australia’s goods trade surplus widened to about A$2.8 billion in September, the largest in seven months
  • That was up from A$184 million in August and well above forecasts
  • Exports rose 2.3% from the month before, led by other mineral fuels, including LNG, and metals
  • Imports fell 3.3%, driven by a nearly 35% drop in gold imports
  • Higher fuel prices have yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill

Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday.

The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less.

Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand.

Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree.

The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months.

At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports.

The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter.

Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan services PMI edges up to 51.7, but composite slips to five-month low as hiring slows
item.description:
The data offer something for both sides of the BoJ debate: historically sharp cost pressures support further tightening, while slowing hiring and weaker confidence give the cautious camp ammunition. On balance, the release is unlikely to shift December pricing materially, leaving the yen more sensitive to the BoJ minutes and oil-driven inflation signals. Firms citing inflation as a drag on confidence underlines how energy costs from the Middle East are feeding into Japanese business sentiment. Weak export orders point to limited support from overseas demand.

--

Earlier:

  • BoJ minutes: board backed further hikes, flagged 50% oil surge as government urged caution

--

Japan’s service providers are still growing and still paying up, but they’re hiring less and feeling gloomier about it.

Summary:

  • The services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3, a fifth month of expansion, driven by domestic demand
  • The composite PMI slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, a five-month low, as manufacturing growth slowed
  • Services hiring rose at the slowest pace in 14 months; across the private sector, job creation hit a one-year low
  • Input cost inflation eased to an eight-month low but stayed well above its long-run average
  • Services confidence fell to its weakest since March, citing inflation, ageing and labour shortages
  • S&P Global said growth momentum and cost pressures will be key for BoJ tightening decisions

Japan’s services sector grew at a slightly faster pace in October, but a slowdown in manufacturing pulled overall private sector growth to a five-month low, while still-sharp cost pressures kept inflation in focus for the Bank of Japan, according to S&P Global’s latest survey.

The S&P Global Japan Services PMI rose to 51.7 in October from 51.3 in September, marking a fifth straight month of expansion. Firms said stronger inflows of new work and efforts to broaden their customer base lifted activity, though growth remained modest and below the average so far this year.

New orders also picked up slightly, driven by firmer domestic demand. Export business fell again, although the decline was the smallest in six months.

Hiring was the weak spot. Services employment rose only marginally, the slowest pace in the current 14-month run of job creation, as some firms reported staff leaving through resignations and retirements. With capacity stretched, backlogs of work increased again.

Price pressures slowed but stayed elevated. Input cost inflation fell to an eight-month low and output charges also rose more slowly, yet both remained well above their long-run averages. Business confidence about the year ahead dropped to its weakest since March, with firms citing inflation, an ageing population and labour shortages.

The broader picture was softer. The composite PMI, which combines services and manufacturing, slipped to 52.1 from 52.3, its lowest since May, though it still pointed to a 19th consecutive month of growth. Faster services growth was offset by a slower rise in factory output. Across the private sector, job creation slowed to a one-year low and confidence fell to a three-month low. Input costs rose at a historically sharp rate, while growth in prices charged eased to a four-month low.

S&P Global said input costs and selling prices, while rising more slowly, were still increasing at a pace that suggests official consumer inflation could stay elevated in the coming months. It added that whether growth loses further momentum and whether cost pressures ease will be key considerations for the BoJ as it weighs further tightening, warning that persistent inflation weighed on confidence and could also constrain demand and hiring.

The data arrive on the same day as minutes from the BoJ’s September meeting, which showed policymakers agreed on the need for further rate increases, keeping attention on whether the central bank moves again in December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6783 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Earlier this week:

  • China’s PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD

-

The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ minutes: board backed further hikes, flagged 50% oil surge as government urged caution
item.description:
The minutes add a hawkish edge to the yen outlook, with talk of a faster pace and getting closer to neutral “relatively soon” supporting pricing for a December move. Against that, one member’s view that market expectations are running ahead of the economy may cap how far rate pricing extends, particularly at the longer end of the JGB curve. Oil is now an explicit driver of BoJ thinking, so renewed crude strength from the Middle East is likely to feed directly into Japanese rate expectations. The Cabinet Office’s call for caution is a reminder that political resistance to rapid tightening remains a factor.

-

The BoJ board in September was arguing over how fast to go, not whether to keep going, with oil doing much of the persuading.

Summary:

  • Members agreed the BoJ should keep raising rates as underlying inflation approached 2% and financial conditions stayed accommodative
  • Several saw a shift in policy phase, from lifting inflation to stabilising it around 2%; one said hikes may need to speed up if prices overshoot
  • One member said hasty action was unnecessary; dissenters Asada and Sato preferred holding at 1%
  • Crude was up about 50% since July, and a few members flagged the tail risk of physical oil shortages
  • The Cabinet Office urged careful examination of the cumulative effects of past hikes
  • The BoJ has since held at 1.25% in October, saying underlying inflation reached levels consistent with its target

Bank of Japan policymakers agreed at their September meeting that the central bank should keep raising interest rates, with some members arguing for a faster pace if prices threaten to overshoot, according to minutes released on Thursday that also showed the government urging caution over the cumulative effect of past hikes.

At the September 17 and 18 meeting, the BoJ raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, in a 7-2 vote. The minutes show members agreed it was appropriate to keep lifting rates and adjusting the degree of monetary accommodation, given that underlying inflation was approaching 2% and financial conditions remained accommodative.

Several members pointed to a shift in the phase of policy. One said the aim was no longer to push underlying inflation higher but to stabilise it around 2%. Another said the BoJ should show markets its determination to prevent prices overshooting by responding nimbly to overseas conditions. A third said the bank would need to speed up its rate hikes if signs of an upward deviation in prices emerged, while another favoured bringing rates closer to the neutral level relatively soon to leave room to move in either direction.

Not all were in a hurry. One member said underlying inflation was not accelerating fast enough to risk the bank falling behind the curve, so hasty action was unnecessary. The two dissenters, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, preferred to hold at 1%. Asada argued that with core inflation below 2%, the economy could not necessarily be called strong, while Sato said economic and price trends had not substantially accelerated.

Oil featured heavily. One member noted crude prices had risen about 50% since July while the yen had appreciated about 5%, which would push up consumer prices considerably if sustained. A few members flagged the tail risk of physical shortages of crude, not just higher prices, citing the suspension of Saudi Arabia’s pipeline operations, unstable shipping through the Red Sea and falling reserves in the US and China.

Members also debated the neutral rate. One noted that a market gauge of the expected peak in rates had risen above 2%, while another said market expectations for hikes appeared somewhat ahead of the economy.

The government’s representatives struck a more cautious tone. The Cabinet Office said the BoJ should examine carefully the cumulative effects of past hikes, consider its neutral rate estimates and act appropriately in the event of excessive swings in the economy and markets.

Since the meeting, the BoJ held rates at 1.25% in October, while saying underlying inflation had reached levels consistent with its target. The minutes reinforce that the debate is over the pace of further tightening, not its direction, keeping attention on the December meeting.

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AstraZeneca makes $10 billion offer for obesity drugmaker Rhythm, WSJ reports
item.description:
The roughly 13% gap between Rhythm’s close and the reported offer price leaves room for a further move if talks are confirmed, but also reflects the risk that no deal materialises. The report is likely to lift interest in other mid-sized obesity and rare disease biotechs as potential targets, given the appetite large drugmakers are showing for the space. For AstraZeneca, a deal of this size is unlikely to move its shares materially but would signal it is willing to buy growth to hit its 2030 target. Chinese drug developers that have licensed obesity assets to Western groups may also draw attention as part of the same deal flow.

- AstraZeneca is reaching for a niche corner of the obesity boom, and paying a premium to get there.

Summary:

  • AstraZeneca made an offer of around $10 billion, or $124 a share, for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals last month, the WSJ reported, citing people familiar with the matter
  • Rhythm shares jumped 28% to just over $110, valuing the company at about $7.6 billion
  • Rhythm develops treatments for rare forms of obesity, including an approved drug for acquired hypothalamic obesity
  • A deal would add to AstraZeneca’s obesity pipeline and its rare disease business built on the Alexion acquisition
  • AstraZeneca targets $80 billion in sales by 2030, up from about $59 billion last year

AstraZeneca has made an offer of around $10 billion for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, in a move that would deepen the British drugmaker’s push into both obesity and rare disease treatments.

According to the report, AstraZeneca offered $124 a share for the US biotech last month, having previously expressed interest in the company. Rhythm’s shares were trading at around $95 on Wednesday afternoon before the report, implying a premium of roughly 30%. They closed up 28% at just over $110, valuing Rhythm at about $7.6 billion. The report did not include comment from either company, and the offer has not been confirmed.

The gap between Rhythm’s closing price and the reported offer, at roughly 13%, suggests investors see some uncertainty over whether a deal will be agreed on those terms.

Rhythm develops treatments for rare forms of obesity linked to the MC4R pathway, which regulates feelings of hunger. When the pathway malfunctions, it can trigger extreme, persistent hunger that leads to severe obesity. The company’s medicines include a treatment approved for acquired hypothalamic obesity, a rare condition.

The fit with AstraZeneca is twofold. The company has been building an obesity pipeline as it seeks a foothold in one of the fastest-growing areas of the drug market. It is developing several GLP-1 treatments, including one licensed from China’s Eccogene for about $185 million in 2023, and in January licensed a set of obesity and diabetes programmes from CSPC Pharmaceuticals, also based in China, for $1.2 billion upfront.

Rhythm would also add to AstraZeneca’s rare disease portfolio, which it built into a leading position through its $39 billion acquisition of Alexion in 2021.

The approach fits a broader strategy. AstraZeneca, valued at close to $300 billion and best known as a cancer drug powerhouse under Chief Executive Pascal Soriot, is targeting $80 billion in annual sales by 2030, up from about $59 billion last year. Analysts say deals will be needed to supplement its pipeline if it is to reach that goal.

A deal of around $10 billion would be modest relative to AstraZeneca’s size, but meaningful for a specialist obesity player, and would underline how large drugmakers are turning to acquisitions to secure growth. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman Sachs: 45% of planned US data centre capacity faces state pauses, but likely short-lived
item.description:
The note gives investors a framework for Wednesday’s selloff in AI infrastructure stocks: a delay story rather than a demand collapse, which may limit further downside if pauses prove brief. A pull-forward of spending into 2027 could support near-term orders for chipmakers and power equipment suppliers, including Asian manufacturers tied to the buildout. Companies with power and permits already secured may gain relative value as new approvals slow. The main risk to the view is that pauses run longer than expected, which would shift the hit from timing to capacity.

---

Goldman sees the political backlash against data centres as a speed bump for the AI buildout, and possibly a reason to build faster before it arrives.

Summary:

  • Goldman estimates states likely to tighten data centre rules hold about 45% of planned US capacity
  • It expects temporary pauses in Texas, Georgia and Michigan while lawmakers weigh rules on power, water and tax breaks
  • Texas alone accounts for roughly a quarter of planned capacity
  • Goldman expects curbs to be short-lived, as data centres aren’t a top voter priority
  • Strategist Rich Privorotsky suggested some companies could pull spending into 2027 to beat new rules
  • The note follows a sharp fall in US AI infrastructure stocks on Wednesday

Goldman Sachs estimates that states likely to tighten rules on data centres account for about 45% of planned US capacity, flagging a new layer of risk for the AI infrastructure buildout after Democrats made gains in this week’s elections, though it expects any restrictions to prove temporary.

The bank’s economists expect Democrats in Texas, Georgia and Michigan to impose short-term pauses on new data centre projects while lawmakers consider tighter rules on electricity use, water consumption and tax incentives, according to reports of the note. Texas alone accounts for roughly a quarter of planned US capacity, making it the most significant of the three.

Goldman does not expect the curbs to last long, reasoning that data centres are not a top priority for voters and that political pressure is likely to ease once new frameworks are in place. That makes the risk one of timing rather than a lasting threat to capacity.

The timing effect may not run in the obvious direction. Goldman strategist Rich Privorotsky suggested some companies could bring spending forward into 2027 to get projects under way before new rules take effect, which could lift investment in the near term even as the medium-term pipeline faces delays.

The warning lands amid a sharp reassessment of the sector. US AI infrastructure stocks fell on Wednesday even as the broader market rallied, and other analysts have moved quickly to quantify the exposure, with one estimate putting more than 13 gigawatts of announced projects in Texas at risk. Several research houses have also cut price targets on companies that had been repositioning toward hosting AI workloads.

Goldman’s emphasis on state-level decisions echoes a view shared across much of this week’s research. UBS also highlighted state governments as more consequential for data centre projects than the change in control of Congress, even as it raised its AI capital spending forecasts.

The global significance lies in the supply chain. US data centre construction drives orders for chips, power equipment and cooling systems worldwide, so delays or a pull-forward in US projects would ripple through suppliers well beyond American borders. The key question now is how quickly states move, and whether pauses stay as short as Goldman expects. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: ADNOC denies report of third Hormuz bypass pipeline that could open to other producers
item.description:
A shared bypass line would chip away at the Hormuz risk premium over time by giving Gulf producers beyond the UAE a route to market that avoids the strait. With ADNOC’s denial, though, the report is unlikely to move crude near term, and the risk premium stays anchored to shipping attacks and transit volumes through the strait itself. The 2027 second line is the more tangible supply factor, potentially easing Asian buyers’ exposure to Hormuz disruption. Repeated attacks on Fujairah also limit how much comfort traders can take from bypass capacity, keeping the infrastructure itself part of the risk.

- The pipeline ADNOC says isn’t happening would have turned the UAE from a country avoiding Hormuz into one selling a way around it.

Summary:

  • Bloomberg reported ADNOC is weighing a third pipeline from the UAE’s west coast to Fujairah, bypassing Hormuz
  • The line could be open to third parties and was described to some Asian customers, but plans are not final
  • ADNOC called the report inaccurate and purely speculative
  • An existing line carries about 2 million barrels a day, and a second line due in 2027 would roughly double capacity
  • The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are all pursuing ways to reduce reliance on the strait
  • Fujairah and Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline have both been attacked during the war

Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. has denied a report that it is weighing a third crude pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a project that, according to Bloomberg, could be opened to other producers and turn the UAE’s east coast into a wider export outlet for Gulf oil.

Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter, that ADNOC was considering a new line from the UAE’s western coast to the port of Fujairah, which sits outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman. The pipeline could be made available to third parties, and ADNOC had described the plan to some Asian customers, the report said, adding that the project was not finalised and its route could change. No cost or timeline was given.

ADNOC told Bloomberg the report was inaccurate and purely speculative.

The third-party element is what sets the report apart from the UAE’s existing bypass strategy. ADNOC already operates a pipeline from its western onshore fields to Fujairah with capacity of about 2 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg, and said in May it was accelerating a second line due for completion in 2027 that would roughly double that capacity. Both serve ADNOC’s own exports. A line open to other shippers would instead position Fujairah as a regional route around Hormuz, extending the UAE’s reach beyond its own production.

That would fit the direction the UAE has taken since leaving OPEC in May, with plans to invest in pipelines, rail, roads and at least three eastern ports to reduce its reliance on the strait. Neighbours are moving the same way: Saudi Arabia plans to expand its East-West pipeline, and Kuwait is in talks with both countries about alternative routes.

The backdrop explains the urgency. Hormuz was almost shut at the height of the Iran war, and while traffic has picked up, ships are still frequently targeted. Bypass routes are not immune either. Fujairah has been attacked several times during the conflict, and Saudi Arabia’s East-West line was briefly halted after an attack in September.

With ADNOC rejecting the report, the plan remains unconfirmed. The more concrete milestone for oil markets is the second pipeline, which ADNOC has told some Asian refiners could supply cargoes at Fujairah from early 2027. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SNB watches for second-round Swiss inflation effects as December rate hike bets build
item.description:
The comments are likely to firm pricing for a December hike, which would mark a turn from the lowest policy rate among major central banks and could lend support to the Swiss franc. With fuel and heating costs driving the jump, the oil price is now a direct input to Swiss rate expectations, tying SNB policy more closely to developments in the Middle East. A franc-supportive shift would also reduce one of the main channels through which the SNB has historically leaned against imported inflation. Traders will watch wage and rent data for the second-round effects Schlegel flagged as the trigger for a more forceful response.

---

Swiss inflation is still inside the SNB’s target, but the speed of the move has caught the bank’s attention, and its chairman wants markets to know it.

Summary:

  • SNB Chairman Martin Schlegel said October’s 1.5% inflation was higher than even the central bank expected
  • The rise, the highest in nearly three years, was driven mainly by fuel and heating costs, with clothing, food and footwear also up
  • The SNB will watch closely for second-round effects on wages and rents, though none of significance have appeared yet
  • Schlegel said the SNB won’t hesitate to adjust policy if price stability is at risk
  • Economists have raised expectations for a hike from 0% at the December 10 meeting

Swiss National Bank Chairman Martin Schlegel said the central bank was caught off guard by the recent jump in Swiss inflation, and signalled it is ready to adjust policy if price stability comes under threat, according to Reuters, citing an interview with newspaper Handelszeitung published on Thursday.

Swiss consumer prices rose 1.5% in October from a year earlier, government data showed on Tuesday, the highest rate in nearly three years. Schlegel said the reading came in above even the SNB’s own expectations and that inflation had risen since the bank’s last policy assessment.

He attributed the increase mainly to higher fuel and heating costs, though prices for clothing, food and footwear also climbed during the month.

The SNB targets annual inflation of between 0% and 2%, so October’s reading remains inside its range. The concern is less the level than the direction and breadth of price pressures. Schlegel said the bank would monitor the situation closely, paying particular attention to whether higher prices begin feeding into other parts of the economy, such as wages and rents.

So far, he said, there had been no significant evidence of those so-called second-round effects, though he could not rule them out in future. He added that the SNB would not hesitate to change its monetary policy should price stability be put at risk.

The remarks carry weight because of where Swiss policy currently sits. The SNB’s policy rate of 0% is the lowest among major central banks, and the October data had already led economists to raise expectations that the bank could lift rates at its next meeting.

Schlegel’s comments stopped short of committing to a move, but his acknowledgement that inflation has surprised the bank, combined with an explicit readiness to act, is likely to reinforce that view. The SNB’s next policy decision is due on December 10.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citrini warns AI infrastructure risk has turned to the downside
item.description:
The split gives both sides of Wednesday’s rotation a research anchor, which may keep AI infrastructure stocks volatile as investors weigh which camp the next earnings season supports. Names exposed to data centre construction and power appear most vulnerable to the state-level permitting and cost risks both houses flag. Hyperscaler debt issuance is a pressure point to watch, given Citrini’s concern about softening demand for those securities. In Asia, the debate feeds directly into AI-linked heavyweights such as SoftBank, where sentiment toward the global buildout drives pricing.

---

UBS and Citrini agree on where the AI risk lives, and disagree completely on how big it is.

Summary:

  • UBS raised its AI capex forecasts to $1.0 trillion for 2026 and $1.4 trillion for 2027, saying demand remains strong
  • Citrini says AI capex growth has peaked, with hyperscaler spending near $1 trillion against AI revenue of at least $200 billion
  • Citrini sees downside risk from hyperscaler issuance, slowing backlog growth and AI price cuts
  • Both see state-level decisions, notably in Texas, as more important for data centres than control of Congress
  • Citrini warns of a shift toward late-cycle stagflation; UBS stays constructive on equities but urges trimming tech concentration
  • AI infrastructure stocks fell sharply on Wednesday even as the broader US market rallied

Two prominent research houses have read the US election results and reached opposite conclusions on the AI spending boom, with UBS raising its capital expenditure forecasts while Citrini Research says growth in AI infrastructure investment has already peaked.

UBS has lifted its aggregate AI capex forecasts to $1.0 trillion for 2026 and $1.4 trillion for 2027, arguing that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong. It does not expect tighter congressional oversight following the Democrats’ wins to derail the investment cycle, since broad federal restrictions would face both legislative and presidential hurdles. It does, however, note that investors are paying closer attention to the risks around overinvestment, financing and monetisation, and expects volatility to stay elevated.

Citrini takes a far more cautious view. In its latest State of the Themes report, published on Wednesday, it argues that annualised hyperscaler capex is approaching $1 trillion while revenue across the AI ecosystem is at least $200 billion, a gap it doubts can be closed. It points to slowing backlog growth, heavy debt and equity issuance by the largest technology companies and price cuts by AI providers as signs of strain, and says the balance of risk for AI infrastructure has shifted to the downside.

The two do agree on where the political risk sits. Both see state-level decisions as more important for data centres than the change in control of Congress. UBS highlighted the composition of state governments, including the result in Texas, as potentially more consequential for individual projects. Citrini went further, treating governor races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia as a referendum on the buildout and expecting higher costs from local concessions, clean energy requirements, ratepayer protections and slower permitting. It cited a Texas moratorium that halted a project linked to $15 billion in bridge loans.

The debate is already showing up in prices. On Wednesday, US stocks rallied broadly while AI infrastructure names fell sharply, with Nvidia down about 3% and Micron and Marvell down around 7%, according to investingLive.

Citrini also warned that the broader macro backdrop is shifting toward late-cycle stagflation, noting that most of the asset pairs it tracks now lean that way and that cyclical stocks have underperformed defensives over the past six months. UBS, by contrast, remains constructive on equities, citing strong earnings, though it recommends investors trim oversized technology exposure.

For investors, the split leaves the AI trade resting on a single question: whether revenue can grow fast enough to justify the spending.

Citrini Research is a thematic investment research firm founded by James van Geelen, which publishes largely through a subscription newsletter with hundreds of thousands of subscribers. It drew wide attention in February, when a viral scenario piece on the economic disruption AI could cause was linked to a selloff in AI-related stocks, Bloomberg reported. In September, chip and data centre research firm SemiAnalysis acquired Citrini, with van Geelen staying on as chief executive.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Citi targets $5,000 gold as a Hormuz reopening could flip the Fed from hikes to cuts
item.description:
The call places oil at the centre of the gold outlook, making Brent and Hormuz shipping headlines the lead indicators for bullion rather than conflict escalation itself. Any sustained drop in crude would likely flow quickly into rate expectations, with Fed pricing the main transmission channel to watch. Until then, the near-term risk for gold stays tied to energy-driven inflation and Fed hike expectations. For positioning, the view argues for treating de-escalation headlines as potentially bullish for gold, a reversal of the usual haven playbook.

Info via note doing the rounds ICYMI. 

For Citi, gold’s next bull run starts not with a crisis but with the end of one.

Summary:

  • Citi has a 0-3 month gold target of $4,500 an ounce and a 6-12 month target of $5,000
  • The forecasts assume the Strait of Hormuz reopens and the Yemen/Saudi conflict de-escalates by year-end
  • Max Layton says much lower oil prices could shift the Fed from hiking to cutting rates
  • That would lift investment demand and could reignite a global momentum rally, supported by existing structural tailwinds
  • Gold has been pressured through the conflict as high oil fed inflation and Fed tightening expectations
  • Gold hit a record near $5,600 in late January, before the war began

Citi sees significant upside for gold if the Strait of Hormuz reopens and the conflict involving Yemen and Saudi Arabia eases, arguing that a resulting slump in oil prices could push the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates to cutting them.

The bank has set a 0-3 month gold target of $4,500 an ounce and a 6-12 month target of $5,000, according to Reuters, with its forecasts assuming the strait reopens and the conflict de-escalates by year-end.

In a research note, Max Layton, global head of commodities research at Citi, said much lower oil prices could prompt that shift in Fed policy, lifting investment demand for gold and reviving a global momentum-driven bull market. He added that such a rally would be supported by several structurally bullish forces already in place.

The call turns on how gold has traded through the Middle East conflict. Rather than rallying as a haven on escalation, gold has come under pressure as disruption to oil flows through Hormuz kept energy prices high. Elevated oil prices feed into inflation, which in turn keeps the Fed leaning toward tighter policy. Higher interest rates and real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding gold, which pays no income, weighing on investor demand even as geopolitical risk rises.

Citi’s argument is that a reopening of the strait would reverse that chain. A fall in oil prices would ease inflation pressure, give the Fed room to lower rates and pull down yields, conditions that have historically favoured bullion.

The shift would be significant for a market that has struggled for much of the year. Gold hit a record high near $5,600 an ounce in late January, before the US-Iran war began at the end of February, and has since traded well below that peak. Citi’s longer-term target would recover a large part of that ground without reclaiming the record.

The view also implies a different reading of gold’s role. In this conflict, the metal has behaved less like a crisis hedge and more like an asset tied to the outlook for interest rates, which means de-escalation, rather than escalation, is the scenario Citi sees as most supportive.

The outlook therefore depends heavily on events in the region. A sustained reopening of Hormuz and a durable easing of hostilities would be the key signals that the conditions Citi describes are taking shape.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS raises AI capex forecast to $1.4 trillion, flags 2027 debt ceiling as key bond risk
item.description:
The note offers a counterweight to Wednesday’s rotation out of AI and chip stocks, arguing that the political risk to data centre spending is more likely to come from state and local decisions than from Washington. For bonds, the risk is skewed toward the long end, where any upswing in deficits and Treasury supply would be felt most, supporting a preference for shorter maturities. Debt-ceiling brinkmanship next year is the event risk to watch for volatility across rates and equities. For investors already overweight AI names, the guidance favours using dips to rebalance rather than to exit.

-

UBS sees more gridlock than upheaval from the midterms, with the real fights coming over debt and the AI boom still intact.

Summary:

  • UBS sees the midterm result as a setback for President Trump and the Republicans, but not a broad Democratic policy mandate
  • It expects more legislative friction rather than a reversal of the administration’s agenda, with the president retaining his veto and wide executive powers
  • 2027 debt-ceiling talks are flagged as the clearest bond risk, with potential for wider deficits, more Treasury supply and brinkmanship-driven volatility
  • The bank still expects inflation to ease, the Fed to finish hiking and yields to settle lower
  • AI capex forecasts raised to $1.0 trillion for 2026 and $1.4 trillion for 2027, with state rules seen as more important than Congress for data centres
  • UBS stays constructive on equities but recommends reducing single-stock concentration and oversized tech exposure, and favours short- to medium-term high-quality bonds

UBS says the 2027 debt-ceiling negotiations are now the clearest risk for US bonds following the midterm elections, while arguing that a Democratic-controlled Congress is unlikely to derail the AI investment cycle, which it expects to keep expanding into next year.

In a note following the vote, the bank described the outcome as a setback for President Trump and the Republicans, and stronger than markets had expected, but cautioned against reading it as a broad mandate for Democratic policy. It expects the result to create more friction in the legislative process rather than a sharp change in direction, noting that the president keeps his veto, Senate rules limit sweeping tax or spending bills, and the executive branch retains wide authority over tariffs and foreign policy.

On debt, UBS sees the coming debt-limit talks as the main pressure point. It suggests the negotiations could lead to planned cuts to social programs being scaled back and defense spending rising, a combination that could undo an expected narrowing of the deficit and add to Treasury supply. Brinkmanship over the talks could also lift bond market volatility. Even so, the bank expects inflation to ease, the Federal Reserve to complete its rate-hiking cycle and Treasury yields to settle lower over time.

On AI, UBS argues that tighter congressional oversight would not necessarily slow investment, since broad federal restrictions would face both legislative and presidential hurdles. It sees state and local rules, including the outcome in Texas, as more important for the timing and location of individual data centre projects. The bank has raised its aggregate AI capital expenditure forecasts to $1.0 trillion for 2026 and $1.4 trillion for 2027, though it notes investors are paying closer attention to the risks of overinvestment, financing and monetisation, and that higher volatility may persist.

For equities, UBS expects the result to drive near-term swings, particularly in technology and other sectors exposed to regulatory scrutiny, but does not see grounds for an immediate strategic shift in portfolios. It remains constructive on stocks, citing strong earnings, while recommending investors reduce single-stock concentration, trim oversized technology exposure and favour quality names across the AI value chain. It views politically driven weakness as an opportunity to rebalance or build positions gradually.

In fixed income, the bank sees value in high-quality bonds with short to medium maturities, but remains cautious on the longest maturities given persistent deficits and heavy issuance. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: SoftBank faces two hits as Arm slide meets US rotation out of AI, leaving Nikkei exposed
item.description:
The divergence on Wall Street sets up a likely split in Tokyo, where AI-linked heavyweights could trail even as the broader market draws support from strong global risk appetite. Falling oil is a modest positive for energy-importing Japan, but a weaker dollar raises the prospect of a firmer yen, a headwind for exporters. The BoJ minutes add a second potential yen driver before the cash open. Traders looking for a relative-value signal will focus on the Nikkei-Topix spread, which tends to widen when AI and chip names diverge from the rest of the market.

---

  • Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts

---

Wall Street gave Tokyo a strong lead, just not for the stocks the Nikkei leans on most.

Summary:

  • Arm fell about 5% in the regular session and slid further after hours despite beating Q2 forecasts
  • US indexes rallied sharply on Wednesday, with the Dow up about 1,570 points, but AI infrastructure stocks fell, with Nvidia down about 3% and Micron and Marvell down around 7%
  • The selloff was linked to concern that tighter restrictions could slow data centre expansion
  • SoftBank holds roughly 90% of Arm and has been among the biggest single drivers of the Nikkei
  • The price-weighted Nikkei is more exposed to an AI selloff than the broader Topix
  • A weaker dollar and the BoJ minutes add a yen dimension to the session

SoftBank Group goes into Thursday’s Tokyo session facing pressure from two directions: a post-results slide in Arm Holdings, which it controls, and a sharp rotation out of AI and chip stocks on Wall Street that left the broader market higher but the AI trade under strain.

Arm shares fell about 5% in the regular session and were around 4% lower again after hours, even though the chip designer beat expectations for its fiscal second quarter. Adjusted earnings per share came in at 52 cents against forecasts of 47 cents, and revenue of about $1.44 billion topped estimates near $1.38 billion. Guidance for the current quarter only edged past consensus, however, and annualised contract value, a measure of licensing commitments, was marginally below expectations.

The regular-session drop fits a wider pattern. US indexes rallied strongly on Wednesday, with the Dow surging about 1,570 points, or roughly 3%, as markets weighed the implications of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress, according to investingLive. The gains were broad, helped by lower Treasury yields, a weaker dollar and falling oil. AI infrastructure stocks went the other way: Nvidia fell about 3%, while Micron and Marvell lost around 7%, amid concern that tighter restrictions could slow data centre expansion and the spending that supports chip suppliers.

That combination matters for Japan because of ownership and index structure. SoftBank holds roughly 90% of Arm, and it has become one of the most influential stocks in the Nikkei 225. It overtook Toyota as Japan’s most valuable company in June, when its rally was the largest single contributor to the index topping 67,000 for the first time. In May, a roughly 5% fall in SoftBank made it the biggest drag on the index.

Because the Nikkei is price-weighted and leans heavily on high-priced, AI-linked names, it is more exposed to a selloff in that theme than the broader, market-capitalisation-weighted Topix. A session in which most stocks rise while AI heavyweights fall could therefore leave the Nikkei lagging the wider market.

The yen is a further variable. A weaker dollar can lift the Japanese currency, which tends to weigh on exporters, and the Bank of Japan’s September meeting minutes are due shortly before the cash open.

Arm’s upbeat commentary offers some offset, with purchase orders for its AGI CPU data centre processor extending through calendar 2027. The key question is whether SoftBank absorbs both hits in full, and how wide the gap between the Nikkei and the Topix becomes. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Dow surges 1,570 points as investors rotate out of AI and chip stocks
item.description:
US stocks closed sharply higher on Wednesday, with the Dow Industrial Average leading the way with a 3.03% gain. The S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Russell 2000 also advanced, but the Nasdaq 100 lagged as selling in Nvidia and AI infrastructure stocks limited the upside.

The rally followed the Democrats’ election victory in both chambers of Congress. Lower Treasury yields, a weaker dollar and falling oil provided a more supportive backdrop for equity buyers as markets assessed the implications of divided government.

The buyers showed up across much of the market. However, there was a clear dividing line within technology. Microsoft, Amazon and Apple posted strong gains, while a number of companies supplying the AI buildout moved sharply lower.

US closing levels

  • Dow Industrial Average rose 1,570.14 points, or 3.03%, to 53,362.33.

  • S&P 500 rose 119.75 points, or 1.58%, to 7,688.67.

  • Nasdaq Composite rose 364.50 points, or 1.44%, to 25,736.51.

  • Russell 2000 rose 44.51 points, or 1.58%, to 2,856.96.

  • Nasdaq 100 rose 256.90 points, or 0.91%, to 28,437.17.

Market breadth gives the rally more credibility

The gains were supported by broad participation.

In the Dow, 27 stocks advanced and only three declined. S&P 500 advancers outnumbered decliners by 374 to 111, while the Nasdaq recorded 2,022 advancing stocks against 1,202 declining stocks. On the NYSE, the split was 1,301 to 492.

That matters. A rally has a stronger foundation when buyers are participating across a wider group of stocks. Today’s advance reached beyond a handful of heavily weighted technology names.

The Dow’s outperformance and the Russell 2000’s 1.58% gain added to that message. Buyers were making a play across different parts of the market.

Dow gainers: 3M leads a broad advance

The Dow’s 1,570-point rally had broad support, with 27 of its 30 stocks closing higher. 3M led the percentage gainers, while Microsoft, Sherwin-Williams, Home Depot and McDonald’s each advanced more than 6%.

  • 3M: +9.55% to $193.95.

  • Microsoft: +6.68% to $555.80.

  • Sherwin-Williams: +6.64% to $363.50.

  • Home Depot: +6.53% to $355.44.

  • McDonald’s: +6.53% to $280.22.

  • Amazon: +6.12% to $266.03.

  • Apple: +5.31% to $349.51.

  • Nike: +5.21% to $40.49.

The leadership stretched across industrials, technology, home improvement and consumer names. That breadth gave the Dow’s advance more credibility, with buyers making a play across a wide range of businesses.

Magnificent Seven: Five rise, two fall

Microsoft and Amazon led the gains among the Magnificent Seven, with Apple also advancing more than 5%.

  • Microsoft: +6.68% to $555.80.

  • Amazon: +6.12% to $266.03.

  • Apple: +5.31% to $349.51.

  • Alphabet: +3.18% to $288.93.

  • Meta Platforms: +1.44% to $630.00.

  • Nvidia: −3.12% to $200.24.

  • Tesla: −3.34% to $385.19.

The split is important. A higher Nasdaq does not mean every major technology stock is attracting buyers. Nvidia and Tesla moved against the broader market as both lost a friend in the GOP, leaving the Nasdaq 100 trailing the other major indices.

AI infrastructure remains under pressure

Several stocks tied to data centers, networking, power equipment and semiconductors suffered substantial declines.

Investors weighed whether tighter restrictions could slow data center expansion. A slower buildout could reduce spending demands on large technology companies while creating headwinds for suppliers dependent on that investment. That helps explain the different reactions within the AI trade.

Among the notable decliners:

  • Vertiv: −12.89% to $205.55.

  • Eaton: −9.99% to $352.56.

  • CoreWeave: −9.90% to $48.42.

  • Ciena: −9.69% to $271.00.

  • Credo Technology: −9.55% to $136.50.

  • GE Vernova: −9.30% to $832.82.

  • Dell Technologies: −9.06% to $371.41.

  • SanDisk: −7.91% to $1,037.40.

  • Lumentum: −7.86% to $626.71.

  • Marvell: −7.08% to $159.80.

  • Micron: −7.00% to $795.23.

Elsewhere, Datadog fell 14.42% to $188.72, while CVS Health declined 12.54% to $79.95.

For traders in those stocks, the broader rally did little to relieve the selling pressure. The burden remains on buyers to show that they can stabilize their own stocks and sustain a recovery.

Winners extend across several industries

The list of gainers included payments, biotechnology, travel, retail, industrials and medical technology.

  • Block: +15.26% to $87.60.

  • Moderna: +13.11% to $258.38.

  • Lyft: +12.42% to $18.74.

  • AppLovin: +10.69% to $271.75.

  • Newmont: +9.94% to $118.15.

  • Booking Holdings: +9.83% to $170.97.

  • Dollar Tree: +9.64% to $147.00.

  • 3M: +9.57% to $193.99.

  • Stryker: +9.41% to $339.77.

  • Intuitive Surgical: +9.38% to $482.10.

Travel and consumer names also participated, with Alaska Air gaining 8.75%, DoorDash rising 8.33% and Best Buy advancing 8.00%. Barrick Mining added 8.37%, joining Newmont among the stronger performers.

Trading lesson: Use the index as a barometer

Today was a good reminder that the broader market provides context, but each stock still needs its own trading plan.

The Dow rose more than 3%. Nvidia fell more than 3%. Microsoft gained nearly 7%, while Vertiv lost nearly 13%.

Those are very different outcomes within the same session.

Use the index as a barometer for market sentiment. Then use the individual stock’s support, resistance and moving averages to define bias, risk and targets. A strong market can provide a tailwind, but buyers still need to get above their own technical hurdles—and stay above them.

item.title: Snap user count falls short at 495 million as profit beat offsets slight revenue miss
item.description:
The share reaction was not available at the time of writing, but the mix points to a tug of war between margin-focused and growth-focused investors. A user miss tends to weigh more heavily on social media stocks than a small revenue shortfall, because audience size underpins future ad pricing. The in-line holiday-quarter outlook offers little to change sentiment either way. Read-through to other digital advertising names is likely to be limited, given the guidance gives no clear signal on the broader ad market.

---

Earlier:

  • Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light
  • Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts

---

Snap is making more money from the users it has, but it is not finding new ones as fast as the market hoped.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue of about $1.72 billion was a touch below estimates near $1.73 billion
  • Adjusted EBITDA of about $383 million beat forecasts of around $338 million
  • Daily active users reached about 495 million, short of expectations near 499 million
  • Q4 revenue guidance of $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion is broadly in line with the roughly $1.96 billion consensus

Snap delivered a mixed set of third-quarter results, with profitability comfortably ahead of expectations but revenue and user growth falling slightly short, while its fourth-quarter outlook landed broadly in line with forecasts.

The Snapchat owner reported revenue of about $1.72 billion, a touch below the roughly $1.73 billion analysts had expected. Adjusted EBITDA was the standout, coming in at about $383 million against forecasts of around $338 million, a beat of roughly 13%. Delivering a profit beat of that size on revenue marginally below expectations indicates the improvement came from the cost side rather than from stronger sales.

User numbers were softer. Daily active users reached about 495 million, around 4 million short of the roughly 499 million the market had pencilled in. For a business that relies on advertising, audience growth is closely watched as a guide to future revenue, so even a modest shortfall tends to draw attention.

The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to a range of $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion. The $1.97 billion midpoint sits just above estimates near $1.96 billion and implies sequential growth of roughly 13% to 16% from the third quarter, reflecting a seasonally stronger period for advertising.

Taken together, the figures point to a company extracting more profit from its existing business while its user base grows more slowly than expected. That margin strength is encouraging, but the slight misses on revenue and users leave the growth story looking less certain.

That split is likely to shape how investors read the results. A strong margin performance can support the stock in the near term, yet sustained upside usually depends on evidence that both users and advertising revenue are expanding.

The next test will be whether Snap can deliver the upper end of its fourth-quarter range, and whether user growth reaccelerates enough to ease concerns that engagement is levelling off. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Arm shares fall 5% after hours despite Q2 beat as outlook only edges past forecasts
item.description:
A 5% fall on a beat in both earnings and revenue shows how high the bar had been set, with the market treating guidance that only matches consensus as a disappointment. The reaction may weigh on AI-linked chip names in the regular session, where richly valued stocks have little cushion for anything short of a clear upgrade. The AGI CPU order book offers some longer-term support, but near-term trading is likely to be driven by positioning rather than the delivery timeline. A recovery would probably need clearer signs of the new processor’s revenue contribution.

---

Earlier:

  • Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light

---

Arm beat on every headline number, but an outlook that only matched expectations was not enough for a stock priced for more.

Summary:

  • Adjusted EPS of 52 cents beat forecasts of 47 cents; revenue of about $1.44 billion topped estimates near $1.38 billion
  • Q3 revenue guidance of $1.49 billion to $1.59 billion and adjusted EPS of about 56 cents sit marginally above consensus
  • Annualised contract value of about $1.79 billion was slightly below expectations
  • AGI CPU purchase orders extend through calendar 2027, with first commercial deliveries on track for the fourth quarter
  • Partners shipped more than 10 billion Arm-based chips in a quarter for the first time; Arm-based PCs are about 20% of global PC shipments
  • Shares fell about 5% after hours

Arm Holdings shares fell about 5% in after-hours trade despite the chip designer beating expectations for its fiscal second quarter, as investors weighed guidance that only marginally topped forecasts and a slight shortfall in a key licensing measure.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at 52 cents, ahead of the 47 cents analysts had expected, while revenue of about $1.44 billion topped forecasts of around $1.38 billion, a beat of a little over 4%.

Guidance for the fiscal third quarter was close to consensus. Arm expects revenue of $1.49 billion to $1.59 billion, with the $1.54 billion midpoint just above estimates near $1.53 billion, and adjusted EPS of about 56 cents against forecasts of 55 cents. Adjusted operating expenses are expected at around $825 million, broadly in line with expectations.

Annualised contract value, a measure of licensing commitments, came in at about $1.79 billion, marginally below the roughly $1.80 billion expected. The miss was small, but for a stock priced for strong growth, an outlook that merely matches estimates can leave little room for disappointment.

The commentary was more upbeat. Arm said purchase orders for its AGI CPU, its data centre processor, now extend through calendar 2027, and that first commercial deliveries remain on track for the fourth quarter. The product marks a shift for a company that has historically licensed designs to chipmakers rather than selling chips itself, and the order book offers early evidence that customers are committing to it.

Arm also said its partners shipped more than 10 billion Arm-based chips in a single quarter for the first time, and that Arm-based PCs now account for about 20% of global PC shipments, a sign of the architecture extending beyond its smartphone base.

The share reaction suggests investors were looking for a bigger step-up in the outlook than Arm delivered. Attention now turns to whether the AGI CPU deliveries land on schedule and how quickly the processor contributes to revenue, which will be central to whether Arm can justify its growth premium into next year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Qualcomm beats Q4 forecasts, shares slip 2% as profit guidance comes in light
item.description:
The after-hours move suggests investors are pricing the guidance rather than the quarter, with the gap between a firm revenue outlook and a softer earnings range pointing to margin pressure as the key risk. A beat that fails to lift the stock tends to weigh on near-term sentiment across the broader chip complex, particularly for names leveraged to smartphone demand. Asian handset and semiconductor supply-chain stocks may take their cue from how Qualcomm trades at the US open. A sharper sell-off in the regular session would signal that the capex surprise is being read as a drag on returns rather than an investment in growth.

---

Qualcomm cleared the bar for the quarter, but a light earnings outlook and a jump in spending left investors looking past the beat.

Summary:

  • Fiscal Q4 revenue of about $10.4 billion beat expectations of around $10.1 billion
  • Adjusted EPS of $2.17 edged past the $2.16 consensus
  • Handset revenue came in at about $5.1 billion, close to half the total
  • Q1 revenue guidance of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion sits above estimates near $10.5 billion
  • Q1 adjusted EPS guidance of $2.15 to $2.35 has a midpoint below forecasts
  • Full-year capex of about $2.5 billion compared with expectations near $1.9 billion; shares fell around 2% after hours

Qualcomm beat Wall Street forecasts for its fiscal fourth quarter, but its shares slipped in after-hours trade as investors focused on profit guidance that came in a little light and capital spending that ran well ahead of expectations.

The chipmaker reported adjusted revenue of about $10.4 billion, ahead of the roughly $10.1 billion analysts had expected, a beat of a little over 3%. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.17, a cent above the $2.16 consensus. Handset revenue, the company’s largest business, was about $5.1 billion, or close to half of the quarter’s total.

The outlook was more mixed. Qualcomm guided first-quarter revenue to a range of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion, putting the midpoint at around $10.8 billion, comfortably above market expectations of roughly $10.5 billion. Its adjusted EPS guidance of $2.15 to $2.35, however, implies a midpoint of $2.25, below analyst estimates in the high $2.20s to low $2.30s.

That pairing of stronger expected sales with softer expected earnings suggests the pressure in the coming quarter is more likely to sit in costs or margins than in demand. It is the kind of split that tends to draw scrutiny even when the headline numbers beat.

Full-year capital expenditure of about $2.5 billion added to that focus. The figure was around a third higher than the roughly $1.9 billion analysts had pencilled in. Heavier investment can underpin future growth, but it also raises the bar for returns at a time when investors are already questioning the profit outlook.

Shares were down about 2% in after-hours trade, a modest move given the beat on both revenue and earnings, and one that indicates the market was looking past the quarter itself to the guidance.

Attention now turns to management’s explanation of what is driving the step-up in spending and how it sees margins developing, along with how the stock trades once the regular session opens. With handsets still accounting for roughly half of revenue, Qualcomm’s results remain closely tied to the health of the smartphone cycle. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Thursday, November 5, 2026 - we hear from the Bank of Japan
item.description:
BoJ minutes due on the September hike that split the board

The Bank of Japan releases the full minutes of its September 17 and 18 policy meeting at 8:50 a.m. Tokyo time on Thursday, and they cover one of the most consequential decisions of the current tightening cycle.

At that meeting the BoJ raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, on a 7-2 vote. The hike came three months after the previous one, compared with six months between earlier moves.

The dissents drew as much attention as the hike itself. Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato preferred to keep the rate at 1%, with Asada pointing to core inflation below 2% and questioning whether the economy was strong enough to absorb another increase. Sato later said she voted against because consumption lacked momentum and underlying inflation was not picking up pace. Their dissents pushed down the yen as markets read them as a sign that further hikes would face resistance.

The minutes should add depth to the Summary of Opinions released on October 1, particularly on how the majority weighed the pace of tightening now that the rate sits within the BoJ’s estimated 1.1% to 2.5% range for Japan’s nominal neutral rate. Traders will also look for discussion of the upside price risks the bank flagged in July, when it warned of an inflation overshoot from soaring fuel costs, rising import costs from a weak yen and strong AI demand.

Some of that debate has since moved on. At its October meeting the BoJ held at 1.25% in an 8-1 vote, with Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of a hike to 1.5%. Asada and Sato backed the hold. The bank said underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with its price target and accelerated the pace of its ETF sales, while it revised up the price outlook for 2027 to 2.6%.

That makes the September minutes more a record of how the Board reached this point than a fresh signal. Any sign that the majority favoured a quicker pace, however, would add weight to speculation about a December move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
